ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Overlapping of Assignments for Adult Education 
.     *121. DR. GOPALRAO VITHALRAO PATIL: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Directorate of Adult Education and  
the National Institute of Adult Education whose functions overlap  
with each other, and the Rural Development Functional Literacy 
roject have not had the expected impact; and 
(b) if so,  what steps are being proposed to  avoid overlapping/  
duplication of assignments and to make Adult Education a success? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the table of  
the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Streamlining the functions of the Directorate of Adult 
Education and the National Institute of Adult Education has been under the 
consideration of the Government for sometime. However, no decision could 
be taken as the mat ter was under litigation. The court cases having been 
disposed of, the Government has decided in principle to integrate the 
National Institute of Adult Education with the National Council for 
Educational Research and Training. 
The scheme of Rural Functiona l Literacy Project (RFLP) has now been 
subsumed within the overall programme for eradication of illiteracy. 
In order to make adult education a greater success, the Government has 
taken some new initiatives recently and these include integration of the 
phases of Total Literacy and Post Literacy, 
1 

RAJYA SABHA   [3 March, 2000] 
delegation of powers to State Literacy Mission Authorities, enlarging the 
scope of Continuing Education, strengthening of Jan Shikshan Sansthans and 
allowing them to operate in rural areas, revitalizing of State Resource Centres 
for preparation of better teaching learning materials and improved quality of 
training. 
DR. GOPALRAO VITHALRAO PATIL: Hon. Chairman, Sir, I thank you 
for the opportunity given to me. The picture of adult educat ion in.our country 
is hazy. After fifty years of independence, India has the largest number of 
non-literate people i.e., 380 million out of 900 million in the world. The aim 
of the National Literacy Mission was to make 100 million people literate by 
the year 1999. Here also, there is a failure to achieve the target because 447 
million adults are there in our country. The present rate of literacy is 62 per 
cent. It is a very good achievement when compared to 18 per cent at the time 
of independence and 52 per  cent in 1991. Therefore, I commend the 
Government for this achievement. But, there are multiple agencies 
implementing this programme on adult literacy. There is a Directorate of 
Education. There is the Institute of National Adult Education. There is the 
National Literacy Mission and there is the Post- Literacy Campaign, 
Continuing Education and so on and so forth. There are programmes on this 
in each and every State. Therefore, there is a multiplicity of agencies, 
schemes and efforts. Therefore, my first su pplementary is, what are the major 
impediments in implementation of adult education programme and by what 
date will we achieve 100 per cent literacy? I want to know whether the 
Government is integrating the various schemes and co ordinating with various 
agencies in the field of adult education. And, what is the amount of money 
spent on salaries of staff, teachers and on educational aids? What preventive 
steps are taken by the Government to root out malpractices and corruption in 
adult education?

DR. RAJA RAMANNA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to point out that 
universalisation of education is a statement which can be construed as 
centralisation of education. Now, centralisation leads to many problems 
which delay the quick spread of literacy. Sir, each region, each village, has a 
certain specific difficulty in making sure that literacy comes quickly into that 
area. Why I say this is because, being Chairman of a task force in Karnataka, 
I know that you just 
5 

RAJYA SABHA             [3 March, 2000] 
can't start schools there exactly at 9.00 a.m. and finish it at 5.00 p.m. There, 
the children have to find a time which suits them, and you just can't have the 
same old education that you have been giving for the last, I do not know, how 
many years. Even modern things which are usually used in the case of the 
elite can be introduced in a cheap way —like the modern montessori system —
which would be helpful in making people understand mathematics at an early 
stage. We do not have to use the old system of sim ply counting, multiplying 
and all those verv crude methods of the past, bygone age. Now, all this has to 
be introduced; and this cannot be done in an universalised way or centralised 
way, A lot of scope has to be given to the villagers and to the teachers.  Now, 
the teachers are just given directions "do this", and some inspectors come 
once in three months to bully the teachers. But if you appoint a proper 
teacher, you will find that education will spread faster because the proper 
teachers understand better the local problems and requirements of the areas 
and the difficulties of the people concerned. Now, I wish to know the views 
of the Minister on this matter. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, the Government docs not believe in 
centralisation of education. Even for this universalisation of education, as I 
have already remarked in my earUer reply, we are not trying to decentralise 
the adult education programme and the national literacy education 
programme. We have given administrative and financial powers to Slate -level 
bodies, and we are asking them to take it up to the district level bodies I fully 
agree that in a country like India, no centralised education programme can 
succeed. Now, as regards the new analogy and curricula, the NCERT is 
having an exercise. The y have produced a document which is being debated 
by the various education boards, and State Governments. We are trying to 
have a decentralised and cost effective programme. 
SHRI GOPALSINGH G. SOLANKI - We have been having this panicuiar 
Programme of Adult Education right from the day of Independence. We have 
seen the Operation Blackboard, the Adult Education  Programme, night 
schools and  aii  that. 
As far as  the sources  are concerned,  it  is not that we have no 
6 
 

[3 March, 2000]        RAJYA SABHA 
 
teachers and that we have no school now: we have everything. However, 
unfortunately, despite the particular effort for fifty years, we could reach 
today 50.02 per cent literacy, and women are illiterate to the tune of 67 per 
cent. 
I want to ask whether the M inistry is thinking of entrusting the work of 
adult education to primary schools, which can educate elders during night or 
other free time. Teachers can be asked to impart education. This is one thing.  
At the same time, as far as the Education Department i s concerned, there 
can be decentralisation of work. Nowadays there are many private high 
schools. They are run by private trusts. Could they be asked to educate adults 
or impart adult education? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, let me first correct the inform ation 
with the hon. Member. The male and female literacy percentages today are 
73 and 60 per cent respectively, and not 52.1 per cent. 
Secondly, it is correct that there are no schools in various places. The 
Education Guarantee Scheme that was launched by the Central Government 
envisages opening of 1,80,000 more schools. These schools will be located 
mostly in villages, and local teachers will man them, as they understand the 
local conditions, the local language and the local pedagogy.

Statement 
Government is aware of the report which appeared in The Statesman dated 
16.02.2000.' The ICHR has requested the publisher, the Oxford University 
Press, to temporarily withhold the  work of publication of the two volumes 
written by Prof. Sumit Sarkar and Prof. K.N. Panikkar. Typescripts of these 
volumes have been requested for perusal. The Council has stated that the 
purpose is to ensure that the lapses and drawbacks found in an earl ier volume 
are not repeated. As per the agreement executed between the ICHR and the 
Publisher, the copyright and all accompaying legal responsibilities rest with 
the ICHR. The Council in its meeting on 20.12.1999 decided that the 
volumes still to be publis hed should not be sent for publication without 
having been reviewed by the Council.

Appraisal of National Malaria Eradication Programme 
*128. SHRIMATI KAMLA SINHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any appraisal of the Centrally sponsored National Malaria 
Eradication Scheme has been made recently by Government to assess the 
achievements since its introduction in the country; 
(b) if so, what are the shortcomings, if  any, identified  in implementation 
of the Programme; and 
(c) what strategy is contemplated by Government in the light of the 
experience gained, to remove the constraints in implementation of the 
Scheme, to achieve its objectives? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) to (c) CAG's 
performance appraisal of the National Anti -Malaria Programme (NAMP) for 
the period 1992—97 has recently been received in Government. The salient 
features of this Report are: 
(i) The incidence of malaria has shown an increase during the period 
1992—97.  
(ii) The index of surveillance as indicated through the Annual Blood 
Examination Rate, was found to be satisfactory. 
(iii) A shortfall was observed in spraying operations required to control 
the parasites. 
(iv) Deficiencies   were   observed   in   rendering   treatment   in 
malaria cases. 
(v) Staffing of laboratories was deficient. 
Independent of the CAG's evaluation, on the basis of in -house monitoring 
of the programme, Government i ntroduced a new Enhanced Malaria Control 
Project (EMCP) from September, 1997 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2000] 
with World Bank assistance. The Project covers 1045 PHCs in 100 
predominantly tribal districts which are malaria endemic in the States of 
Andhra Pr adesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and 
Rajasthan. It also covers 19 cities/towns having high malaria endemicity 
from these States, as well as in the States of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and 
West Bengal. The salient features of the EMCP are:—  
• Early case Detection and Prompt Treatment (EDPT) through use of 
newer drugs and Rapid Diagnostic Kits. 
• Selective Vector Control including use of Synthetic Pyrethroids in rural 
areas and Biolarvicides in urban areas. 
• Promotion of personal protection me thods by use of Medicated 
Mosquito Nets (MMNs) 
• Early detection and containment of epidemics. 
• Information, Education and Communication towards personal 
prevention and Community participation. 
• Institutional and Management capacity building, manpower 
development through intensive re -orientation training programmes at 
all levels and efficient Management Information System (MIS). 
Under this Project for Human Resource Development (HRD), 
Management Information System (MIS) and Information Education and 
Communication (IEC) activities, the whole country is being covered. 
Moreover, there is flexibility within this Project to divert resources in case of 
any outbreaks or epidemics to any part of the country. 
This Project is in addition to the on -going National Anti Mala ria 
Programme for which both financial/material assistance and technical 
support & guidance is provided to all States and UTs on a sharing basis. For 
the North -Eastern States, 100% central assistance is being provided under 
this Programme from December, 1994. 
34 

[3 March, 2000]      RAJYA SABHA 
 
Annual Programme Development Review (APDR) is an integral part of 
the World Bank assisted project. Besides, regular reviews of the National 
Programme are undertaken from time to time.

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir.

Education Minister's Conference held in October 1998, to pursue universal 
elementary education in a mission mode. 
Education Minister's conference had recommended the pursuit of  Universal 
Elementary Education in a mission mode. A National Committee of 
Education Minister's under the Chairmanship of the Minister, Human 
Resoruce Development was set up on the recommendation of the conference 
to work out the approach to the mission mode. The Committee submitted its 
report in October, 1999. The draft framework for a holistic and convergent 
approach to UEE in the mission mode was circulated to the States for their 
comments. The scheme of Serva Shiksha Abhiyan was revised incorporating 
the suggestions made by the States and then discussed in an Education 
Secretaries Conference in November 1999. The Goals of the SSA are as 
follows;—

(ii) All 6—14 age children complete fiv e year primary education by 2007.

in consultation with Panchayati Raj Instiutions will form the basis of district

registered societies at state level. There will be a focus on districts having 
low female literacy among Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan will cover the entire country with a special focus on 
educational needs of girls. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and other 
children in difficult circumstances.

Improving the quality of Higher Education 
*134 MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOP MENT be pleased 
to state:. 
(a) whether Government have any plans to improve the quality of higher 
education, particularly in the Rural and suburban sectors; 
(b) whether the colleges there are fully funded by the Government; 
(c) whether Government extract qualitative work from the teachers; and 
(d) whether Government have any plans to make colleges in the country self -
supporting and independent of dependence on Government aid? 
39 

  RAJYA SABHA    [3 March, 2000] 
 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MA NOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) Yes Sir. It has always been part of 
Government educational policy to promote quality at all stages of education 
including higher education. The main emphasis has been in the areas of 
access, relevance and quality. The University Gr ants Commission (UGC) was 
set up in 1956 to make provisions for the coordination and determination of 
standards in universities. The • National Policy on Education 1986 and its 
accompanying Programme of Action 1992 have further laid emphasis on this. 
Quality improvement in higher education is sought to be achieved through a 
wide renge of interventions. These include schemes such as Special Assistance 
to College located in Rural Backward Areas, Special Assistance Programme, 
Academic Staff Colleges, Strengthe ning of Infrastructure in Science and 
Technology etc. 
An Inter University Centre namely the National Assessment and 
Accreditation Council was also set up in 1994 so as to look at quality issues 
in the higher education sector. The National Board of Accredit ation has 
similar responsibilities on the technical education side. There is a move to 
make accreditation compulsory in higher educational institutions within a 
definite time frame. 
To give a further boost to the quality of teachers in higher education, the 
Government has also provided for revision of pay scales of the university and 
college teachers with a view to attracting better talent in this area. Colleges 
are being funded as per prescribed norms faid down by the UGC. In so far as 
the colleges under t he State Governments are concerned, there are separate 
funding arrangements for them by the concerned State Governments. 
Government has no intention whatsoever of withdrawing financial support 
to higher education institutions. In fact, the Ninth -Plan allocation for higher 
education has been increased from Rs. 800 crores during the Eighth Plan 
period to Rs. 2000 crores. Universities and colleges are also being 
encouraged as a part of already existing educational policy to become 
financially more resilient so as to upgrade their standards.

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) to (c) Government has 
decided to help the State  Governments in better targetisation of Public 
Distribution System (PDS) and to enhance the food security of the people 
living below poverty line by doubling the quantity of foodgrains from the 
present 10 kg. per family per month. 
PDS is operated under the  joint responsibility of the Central and State 
Governments. The Central Government is responsible for procurement, 
storage and transportation of PDS commodities up to the central godowns 
and making them available to the State Governments. The responsibilit y for 
distribution to the consumer through Fair Price Shops (FPSs) and 
administration of PDS rest'with State Governments/UT Administrations. In 
order to efficiently reach the essential commodities in PDS to the consumers 
in a transparent and accountable ma nner a Model Citizens' Charter for 
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) has also been drawn up and 
circulated to States/UTs for adoption. Based on the belief that truly 
democratic institutions do better safeguard food security concerns of all than 
the State bureaucracy, the Government also have advised the State 
Governments to more substantially involve Gram Panchayats in supervision 
and monitoring of PDS especially at FPS level as a measure of social audit.  
Under the Centrally Sponsored Schemes financial assistance is provided to 
States/UTs for construction of godowns of small capacity up to 2000 MT and 
for purchase of vans/trucks for strengthening PDS. The assistance is given as 
50% grant -in-aid and 50% loan. Financial assistance is also provided for  
organizing training courses for upgradation of skills of officials dealing with 
PDS and for purchase of computer system to link the Directorate of Food & 
Civil Supplies in States/UTs to monitoring network through National 
Informatics Centre (NIC).

responsibility of the Central and State Governments/UT Administrations. 
The Central Government is responsible for procurement, storage and 
transportation of the PDS commodities up, to the central godowns and 
making them available to the States. The responsibility for distribution to the 
consumers through the fair Price Shops and administration of the PDS rests 
with the State Government and UT Administrations. State Government have 
been requested to closely mon itor PDS at the Fair Price Shops (FPSs) and 
other levels and to make arrangement for distribution of PDS commodities in 
a transparent and accountable manner by involvement of Panchayati Raj 
Institutions (PRIs) and consumer organizations in implementation o f PDS. 
They have also been asked to eliminate bogus ration cards and initiate action 
against erring FPS owners under Section 3 of Essential Commodities Act,

the Department of Public Distribution to attend to the

been provided with independent telephon e, fax and e -mail facilities in

attend to public complaints on priority, the Department has also designated 
senior officers of the Department as members of flying squad for co nducting

Government of India also has appointed Area Officers to States/UTs to 
monitor the functioning of Public Distribution System including the 
complaints of diversion.

reviewed in a meeting of the State Food Secretaries first on 10.8.98 and 
subsequent discussions with representatives of the State Governments. Many 
States, while disagreeing with the estimates of diver sion brought out in the 
study, recognized that leakages do take place. Several States stated that 
bogus ration cards were being weeded out in special drives. States like Tamil 
Nadu and Haryana have issued computerised ration cards with photograph of 
the he ad of family to prevent misuse. The State Governments have been 
requested to streamline their delivery system and to take steps to curb the 
diversion and to weed out the bogus units. The State Governments have been 
asked to adopt the Citizen's Charter that  ensures the consumer's right to 
information.

Yamuna water unfit for human consumption 
936. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether according to a survey conducted by CPCB, it has been found 
that the water of Yamuna is not fit for human consumption as reported in th e 
Hindustan Times dated 29th January, 2000; 
(b) if so, whether the Union Government, in consultation with the State 
Government propose to formulate any concrete plans to keep the Yamuna 
free from pollution; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE  IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The 
stretch of river Yamuna in Delhi is polluted between Wazirabad and Okhla 
barrage due to discharge of untreated sewage and industrial effluents and river 
water is not fit for human consumption. Water quality parameters like 
dissolved oxygen, bio- chemical oxygen demand and total coliforms are not 
meeting the desired standards. Under the Yamuna Action Plan, a small 
component of two sewage treatment plants and one electric crematorium only 
are covered, which are targetted for completion by March, 2000. Major works 
of constructing 15 sewage treatment plants to increase the sewage treatment 
capacity from the present 1200 million litres per day to 2300 million litres per 
day has been taken up  by the Government of National Capital Territory of 
Delhi from "their own Plan funds. These works are targetted for completion 
by December, 2000. In addition, the Government of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi has also decided to undertake complete rehabilitation of the 
sewerage system so that all the surface drains presently discharging 
wastewater into the river are intercepted and diverted for treatment to these 
sewage treatment plants. A minimum flow of 10 cubic metres per second o f 
fresh water is desired in the river for which all the riparian States except Delhi 
have agreed to release their share. As a permanent measure to tackle industrial  
102

pollution, the Government of National Capital Territory of  Delhi has decided 
to construct 15 Common Effluent Treatment Plants in 21 industrial estates of 
Delhi which are under implementation. Water quality of Yamuna will

Governments Organisations and others for supporting the Government

trade routes and develop ing a forensic identification reference Manual 
for tiger parts and products. 
9. Funds are being provided to the State Governments for the eco-
development of the areas to reduce the biotic pressure thereon.

†952. SHRI JHUMUK LAL BHENDIA:  Will the Minister of HEALTH

tuberculosis in India, stating the percentage or rate of success of the efforts to

(b) what are the reasons that Government's claim that it have got control 
over this disease, are proving to be hollow; and

†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi.

whether any campaign is bring run to get control over T.B. by settin g any

THE MINISTER O F STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) to (c) India alone 
accounts for 25% of global TB burden and half million people are estimated 
to be dying every year. 
The National TB Control Programme, which is in operation s ince 1962, 
was reviewed in 1992 and the findings of the Review Committee interalia 
were that the treatment completion rate if less than 40%, there were drug 
shortage, emphasis on X -ray for diagnosis, poor quality sputum microscopy, 
multiplicity of treatmen t regimens, inadequate budget and managerial 
capacity etc. 
Based on these findings, Government of India evolved a Revised National 
TB Control Programme with the objective of curing at least 85% of sputum 
positive cases and detecting at least 70% of these cases. This World Bank 
assisted programme, which is in operation since 1993- 94, is expected to 
cover 270 million population by 2000 following the Direct Observation 
Treatment Strategy (DOTS). 
Under RNTCP, quality of diagnosis has been good and sputum conver sion 
rate remains high at 87%. The programme is being expanded in a phased 
manner. It is expected that RNTCP will cover 400 million population by 
2002.

Implementation of Population Policy 
966. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the annual increase of 15.50 
million in Indian population was neutralising our efforts to conserve 
environment or boost development of the country; 
(b) whether it is a is fact  that by May this year, the country is projected to 
have one billion (100 crore) population; 
(c) if so, what steps Government have taken to control the population; and 
(d) whether any National Population Policy, 2000 has been formulated so 
far by Government and if so, in what manner Government have decided
 monitor policy implementation? 
THE-MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The Government has been aware that the annual increase in population 
was neutralising efforts to conserve environment and economic development. 
Government has taken remedial action from time to time under the National 
Family Welfare P rogramme officially launched in 1951. There have been 
significant achievements under the programme and the States like Kerala, 
Tamil Nadu and Goa have already achieved goals set for 2000 AD (i.e. 
replacement level of fertility being 2.1). The States of And hra Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Gujarat and Maharashtra are close to achieving this goal. 
154 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2000] 
(d) The Government of India has approved the National Population Policy 
2000. The Policy seeks to put in place a multi -sectoral agenda for population 
stabilisation which includes increasing out -reach and coverage of 
reproductive and child health care services, strengthening of health 
infrastructure, meeting the unmet needs for contraception services, and 
converging of integrated service deliver y at village and house -hold levels. 
Stabilising population is perceived as much a function of extending primary 
and secondary education, improving access to safe drinking water, sanitation 
and housing, and building roads, and providing transport and 
communication. 
For monitoring implementation of the Policy, the document suggests 
setting up of the following new structures:—  
(i) National Commission on Population.                                                                  
(ii) State/UT Commission on Population.                                                          
(iii) Coordination Cell in the Planning Commission and                                                  
(iv) Technology Mission in the Department of Family Welfare. 
Limiting Population Growth 
967. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country's population will soon cross the one billion mark; 
(b) whether it is now 26th year since the 1st National Population Policy 
was presented to Parliam ent in April, 1976; if so, why that policy has not 
been implemented; and 
(c) what steps Government are planning to limit population growth, which 
is largely diluting the front of our economic development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) The population of 
India is projected to reach the one billion, mark on 11th May, 2000. 
(b) A statement on National Population Policy was made by the 

[3 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
then Minister of Health and Family Plan ning on 16th April, 1976 proposing 
following measures to bring down the growth rate of population. 
(i) Raising the age of marriage to 18 for girls and 21 for boys. Make 
registration of marriage compulsory. 
(ii) Freezing of representation in the Lok Sabha and the State 
Legislature on the basis of 1971 Census till the year 2001. 
(iii) Earmark 8 percent of Central Assistance to State Plan against 
performance in Family Planning. 
(iv) Raising the levels of female education, earmark adequate outlays 
for girl's education upto the middle level and child nutrition. 
(v) Introduction of population values in the educational system. 
(vi) Monitoring of performance of family planning in the States, 
intensively. 
(vii) In depth review of family planning programme in the coun try by 
Union Cabinet at least once in a year. 
(viii) Raising of compensation money for adoption of family planning 
methods to Rs. 150 if performed with two living children or less: 
Rs. 100 if performed with three living children and Rs. 70 if 
performed with four or more children. 
(ix) Introduction of Group Incentive so as to make family planning a 
mass movement with greater community involvement. 
(x) Involvement of Voluntary Organisation for promotion of family 
planning awareness. 
(xi) Limitation after thre e children be made uniformly applicable to all 
Indian Citizens, residents in the States, without distinction of 
caste, creed or community. 
156 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2000] 
(xii) Make changes in service/conduct Rules of Central Government 
employees to ensure that they adopt small family norm. 
(xiii) To adopt multi-media  motivational strategy to spread the messages 
of family planning throughout the nation. 
Another Policy Statement on Family Welfare Programme was made on 
June 29, 1997, which inter -alia focused on the measures proposed in 1976 
Policy. However, it streesed on integration of family planning programme 
with other welfare programme and proposed the change in the name of the 
programme from 'Family Planning' to 'Family Welfare'. 
Both the Statements we re laid on the Table of the House of Parliament, 
but not discussed. However, most of the initiatives except some coercive 
measures were undertaken while giving a new dimension to the 
implementation of the family welfare programme during the Five Year 
Plans, after 1976. 
In 1983, National Health Policy was formulated which provided 
comprehensive framework for planning, implementation and monitoring of 
Health Care Services. This Policy identified priority areas for intervention in 
the next two decades and set goals to be achieved by 2000 A.D. 
Recognising the fact that reduction in infant and child mortality is an 
essential pre -requisite for acceptance of small family norm, Government 
integrated MCH and Family Planning as part of Family Welfare Services at 
all levels. In order to give new trust and dynamism to the ongoing family 
welfare programme, the National Development Council set up a sub -
committee on Population in 1992. The sub -committee gave a report in 1993, 
which was endorsed by NDC. This report recommended that Family Welfare 
Programme should take cognisance of area specific socio -economic, 
demorgraphic and health care availability differentials and allow requisite 
flexibility in planning and implementation. 
The Child Survival and Safe Motherhood (CSSM) programme was 
157 

[3 March, 2000]      RAJYA SABHA 
 
initiated in 1992. The pulse polio initiative aimed at eradication of Polio by 
2000 was initiated in 1996. 
The International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) held 
in Cairo, 1994 led to laun ch of Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) 
Programme in 1997. RCH gave a holistic approach to the whole family 
welfare programme. 
As a result of various programmes Crude Birth Rate (CBR) has reduced 
from 40.8 in 1951 to 26.4 in 1998, IMR has reduced from 146 in 1951 to 72 
in 1998, Couple Protection Rate went up from 10.4% in 1971 to 44% in 
1999, Crude Death Rate (CDR) has reduced from 25 in 1951 to 9.0 in 1998 
and Total Fertility Rate (TFR) has reduced from 6.0 in 1951 to 3.3 in 1997. 
(c) The National Popula tion Policy, 2000 has now been approved by the 
Government. It takes note of all earlier consultations. The National 
Population Policy seeks to put in place a multi -sectoral agenda for population 
stabilisation which includes increasing outreach and coverage of reproductive 
and child health care services, strengthening of health infrastructure, meeting 
the unmet needs for contraception services, and converging of integrated 
service delivery at village and house-hold levels. 
Stabilising population is perceive d also as a function of extending primary 
and secondary education, improving access to safe drinking water, sanitation 
housing, and building roads, and providing transport and communication.

Care and implemented through a network of 447 District TB Centres and 330

including free supply of anti -TB drugs. To cut short the deration of the 
treatment, Short Course Chemotherapy has been introduced in 292 districts. 
This programme was reviewed in 1992 and the findings of the Review 
Committee inter-alia were that the treatment completion rate is less than
